common_name: Kakai Pumpkin (Styrian Hulless-Seed Pumpkin, Oil Seed Pumpkin)

planting.note: Sow seeds directly into warm soil a week or two after the last frost, spacing hills widely to accommodate sprawling vines, and keep beds evenly moist through flowering and fruit set.

directions: Sow seeds directly into warm soil a week or two after the last frost, spacing hills widely to accommodate sprawling vines, and keep beds evenly moist through flowering and fruit set. This Austrian landrace from Styria produces medium orange pumpkins prized not for their stringy flesh but for their thin-hulled, dark-green naked seeds, which are roasted or pressed for the region's famous dark green pumpkinseed oil. Harvest when rinds harden and vines die back, then cure fruit briefly before scooping and drying seeds for eating or oil pressing. It has become a staple specialty crop among home seed-savers and oil producers in North America since the late 20th century.

planting.note: Plant seeds directly outdoors once soil has warmed after the last frost, giving vines plenty of room to ramble, and water deeply but infrequently to encourage strong root development.

directions: Plant seeds directly outdoors once soil has warmed after the last frost, giving vines plenty of room to ramble, and water deeply but infrequently to encourage strong root development. A colonial-era American heirloom closely related to Green Striped Cushaw, this variety bears crookneck-shaped fruit with smooth cream-white rind and pale flesh that is drier and less sweet, making it especially favored for savory cooking and livestock feed. Its resistance to squash vine borer and adaptability to hot, humid conditions kept it popular across the South long before modern butternut types became dominant. Store cured fruit in a cool, dry space where it will keep for several months.

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed near a trellis or open ground where its vigorous, fig-shaped-leaved vines can climb or sprawl, watering regularly during establishment.

directions: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed near a trellis or open ground where its vigorous, fig-shaped-leaved vines can climb or sprawl, watering regularly during establishment. Distinct from other Cucurbita species, this cool-tolerant Andean and Mesoamerican heirloom produces watermelon-striped fruit with black seeds and stringy white flesh traditionally candied into the Mexican sweet cabello de ángel or brewed into a folk remedy. Its unusual cold hardiness for a squash and ability to fruit at higher elevations made it a long-season staple crop from Mexico through the Andes. Fruit stores exceptionally well, often lasting a year or more in cool, dry conditions.

planting.note: Sow directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost, or start indoors in short-season climates and transplant carefully to avoid root disturbance.

directions: Sow directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost, or start indoors in short-season climates and transplant carefully to avoid root disturbance. This heavy-feeding Quebecois heirloom was cultivated by market gardeners around Montreal in the late 1800s and prized for producing enormous, heavily netted, nutmeg-type melons that could reach 10-15 pounds under generous manuring and glass-frame protection. Its green flesh is exceptionally sweet and aromatic, though the variety demands rich soil and a long, warm season to reach its famous size. Nearly lost to commercial cultivation, it survives today largely through heirloom seed-saving networks.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm, spacing hills generously since vines spread widely, and reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars.

directions: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm, spacing hills generously since vines spread widely, and reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars. Originating in the Berry region of central France, this squash produces flattened, deep-orange, lightly ribbed fruit with notably dense, dry, sweet flesh reminiscent of chestnuts, making it a favorite for soups and roasting. It shares ancestry with Musquée de Provence but stays smaller and matures faster, fitting gardens with shorter seasons. Cure fruit in the sun for a week or two after harvest to harden the rind and intensify flavor before storing.

planting.note: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, since this compact bush type needs less room than typical maxima squash and tolerates close spacing well.

directions: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, since this compact bush type needs less room than typical maxima squash and tolerates close spacing well. A traditional South American variety popular in Argentina and Uruguay, it produces small, pale-green, round to slightly ribbed fruit best picked young and tender at 3-4 inches for use in stuffed-squash dishes and stews. Frequent picking every couple of days encourages continued production through the season, much like a zucchini. Its compact habit and rapid maturity make it well suited to smaller garden beds and container growing.
